full_story_part1.text: The alarm has not rung yet. The room is quiet. Then, suddenly, you are awake just before it sounds. It can feel as if the body has somehow read the clock. Research suggests a less magical, but still surprising, explanation. The brain and body keep time through an internal daily system. Light and regular sleep and wake times help set that system. When a waking time is expected, the body may also begin preparing before sleep ends. In a laboratory study, blood levels of ACTH, a hormone, rose about one hour before an expected waking time. Researchers saw this as more than the normal daily rhythm. They said it could be part of a preparation process for the end of sleep.

full_story_part2.text: Other small studies found changes before planned self-awakening. In one, activity in a front part of the brain changed about 30 minutes before waking. In another short-nap study, heart rate began to rise about 3 minutes before waking. But this is not proof that the body can read an alarm with perfect accuracy. Most self-awakening studies asked people to choose a waking time and try to wake then without outside help. That is related to waking just before an alarm, but it is not exactly the same event. The real question is why the feeling can sometimes be so precise.

point_one.text: In one laboratory experiment, weak light and a fixed routine matched a 24-hour day, but usually did not match shorter or longer days of 23.5 or 24.6 hours. Regular mornings may steady the body's timing near its natural, almost-24-hour rhythm. They do not turn it into a countdown timer.

point_two.text: A different clue comes from planned self-awakening. In one study of 11 people, 82% met the study's success rule on day 7 after repeated attempts. Yet about 10% of 643 university students said they routinely self-awoke. This suggests that expectation and practice may matter for some people, while a broadly reliable ability is not established. Most studies tested planned waking, not accidental waking just before a real alarm.
